title: Machine Learning
body:
This course covers what to do when the algorithm cannot be written down. Recognising a
handwritten digit has no procedure anybody can state: there is no rule separating a 4 from a
9 that survives contact with real handwriting.

The method replaces writing the procedure with fitting one. Specify a family of procedures
with free parameters, define a number measuring how badly a given setting of those parameters
performs, and let [[Optimization|optimisation]] search for the setting that makes that number
small. The program is fitted to data, and that shift is what makes the content of the course
[[CALCULUS 1|calculus]], [[LINEAR ALGEBRA|linear algebra]] and [[STATISTICS|statistics]] under
a new vocabulary.

One worked example carries the whole course: a [[Neural Network]] trained by
[[Back Propagation]] on [[MNIST]], taken apart piece by piece. What a [[Neuron]] computes,
what an [[Activation Function]] contributes, what a [[Loss Function]] measures, how
[[Gradient Descent]] moves downhill on it, and how the fitted result is evaluated.

## Topics

### The three choices

Every method in the folder is a choice of three things, and each is independent of the others.

| Piece | What it determines | Examples in this vault |
|---|---|---|
| Model | the family of functions available to fit | [[Linear Regression]], [[Logistic Regression]], [[Multilayer Perceptron]], [[CNN]] |
| Loss | what a wrong answer costs | squared error, [[Log Loss]], [[Cross-Entropy Loss]] |
| Optimiser | how the parameter space is searched | closed form in [[Least Squares]], [[Gradient Descent]], [[SGD Classification\|SGD]] |

Carry that decomposition through the whole course. A question about a technique is usually a
question about which of the three it changed.

[[Classification]] predicts which of a finite set of labels an input belongs to and is the
course's default problem. [[Binary Classification]] is the two-label case, where a single
probability specifies the answer and where the evaluation vocabulary below is defined.
[[Logistic Regression]] is the smallest honest classifier, a linear score squashed into a
probability, which is what a network does at one layer of depth. [[Linear Regression]] in
[[STATISTICS]] is the smallest supervised model of all and the one case where the fit has a
closed form requiring no optimiser. [[MNIST]] supplies the handwritten digits, and
[[Stratification]] is how a dataset is split without distorting the class proportions.

### What a neuron computes

A [[Neuron]] is a small arithmetic expression and nothing more. It takes a [[Dot Product]] of
the inputs against the [[Weights]], adds a [[Bias Term]], and passes the result through an
[[Activation Function]]:

$$
\text{output} = \sigma(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b)
$$

```
inputs   x = [2, 1]
weights  w = [0.5, -1.0]        learned, and the only thing training changes
bias     b = 0.3

w · x + b = (0.5)(2) + (-1.0)(1) + 0.3 = 0.3
σ(0.3)    = 0.574                        squashed into (0, 1)
```

The weights decide how much each input matters and the bias shifts the threshold at which the
neuron responds. Training changes those numbers and changes nothing else.

### Layers, and why a forward pass is matrix multiplication

Neurons in a layer all read the same inputs with different weights, so stacking their weight
vectors as the rows of a [[Matrix]] turns the whole layer into one multiplication:

```
W = [ 1   2 ]      x = [1]        W x = [ (1)(1) + (2)(3) ]  = [  7 ]
    [ 0  -1 ]          [3]              [ (0)(1) + (-1)(3) ]   [ -3 ]

ReLU applied elementwise                                       [  7 ]
                                                               [  0 ]
```

A [[Forward Pass]] is that operation repeated for each layer: multiply, add the bias vector,
apply the activation, hand the result to the next layer. [[Neural Network]] indexes the whole
structure, layers take one of three roles as the [[Input Layer]], a [[Hidden Layer]] or the
[[Output Layer]], and [[Bias]] covers the two unrelated meanings the word carries.

The [[Perceptron]] is the single-layer original and carries the account of what one layer
cannot represent, which is any function whose classes cannot be separated by a straight line,
XOR being the standard case. The [[Multilayer Perceptron]] stacks layers, which is what the
phrase neural network usually means. [[CNN]] is the architecture that exploits spatial
structure in an image by sharing one set of weights across every position, which is what
[[Computer Vision]] needs, since a feature is the same feature wherever it appears in the
frame.

### Why the activation function has to be non-linear

Stack two linear layers and the result is $W_2(W_1 x) = (W_2 W_1) x$, which is a single
matrix. A network of $n$ linear layers therefore has exactly the expressive power of one
layer, and depth buys nothing at all. The [[Activation Function]] supplies the
[[Non-Linear|non-linearity]] that makes the composition worth something.

[[Sigmoid]] squashes its input into $(0,1)$, so the output reads as a probability, and it
saturates at both ends where the gradient approaches zero and learning stalls. [[ReLU]]
computes $\max\{0, z\}$ and is the default for hidden layers, since it keeps a constant
gradient on the positive side and costs one comparison. [[Leaky ReLU]] gives the negative side
a small slope, which addresses the dead unit a ReLU becomes when its input stays negative and
its gradient stays zero forever.

### The loss function

A [[Loss Function]] is the single number being minimised, and it has to be differentiable,
which is what rules out accuracy as a loss. Accuracy changes in steps as predictions flip, so
its gradient is zero almost everywhere and carries no direction to move in.

[[Log Loss]] and [[Cross-Entropy Loss]] are the same function named from the likelihood side
and the information side. For a single example whose true class the model gave probability
$q$:

```
model says 0.9 for the right class   loss = -ln(0.9) = 0.105     small
model says 0.1 for the right class   loss = -ln(0.1) = 2.303     large
```

Confidence in the wrong answer is punished without bound, which is the property that makes it
suitable for [[Classification]].

### Gradient descent

The parameters that minimise the loss cannot be solved for directly once there are a million
of them, so the optimiser walks downhill. Evaluate the [[Gradient]], take a step against it,
repeat:

$$
w \;\leftarrow\; w - \eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial w}
$$

On $f(x) = x^2$, whose derivative is $2x$, starting at $x = 3$ with a learning rate of 0.1:

```
step 1:  3.000 - 0.1(6.000) = 2.400
step 2:  2.400 - 0.1(4.800) = 1.920
step 3:  1.920 - 0.1(3.840) = 1.536      approaching the minimum at 0
```

Each step is a [[Linear Approximation]] trusted for a short distance, and the learning rate
sets how far that trust extends. Too small and training crawls; too large and the step
overshoots the valley and the loss grows.

[[SGD Classification]] estimates the gradient from a small batch of examples, which works
because a minibatch gradient is an unbiased estimate of the full one with a standard error
shrinking as $1/\sqrt{n}$, so a batch of 32 gives most of the accuracy of the full dataset at
a tiny fraction of the cost.

### Backpropagation

[[Back Propagation]] computes the derivative of the loss with respect to every weight, and it
is the [[Chain Rule]] applied through a composition of layers. A weight in an early layer
affects the loss through everything downstream of it, so its derivative is a product of
factors along that path.

The algorithm runs backwards from the output because that order reuses work. The factors
needed for a layer's weights are exactly the ones already computed for the layer above it, so
one backward sweep produces every derivative. Computing them forwards instead would repeat
that shared work once per weight, which is the difference between training a network and
watching it fail to train.

### Evaluating the result

A [[Confusion Matrix]] holds the four outcomes and every rate is computed from its cells.
Testing a spam filter on 100 emails, of which 10 are spam:

```
                    predicted spam    predicted clean
actually spam            8 (TP)            2 (FN)
actually clean           5 (FP)           85 (TN)
```

[[True Positive]], [[True Negative]], [[False Positive]] and [[False Negative]] name the
cells. [[Sensitivity]] is the fraction of spam caught, $8/10 = 0.80$. [[Specificity]] is the
fraction of clean mail correctly passed, $85/90 = 0.944$. Accuracy is $93/100$.

That accuracy figure is why accuracy alone is misleading. A filter that marks everything clean
scores $90/100$ on this data, beating a real attempt at nine out of ten problems while
catching no spam whatsoever. On imbalanced data the majority class dominates the number.
[[Stratification]] preserves the class proportions across a split so the per-cell rates mean
something.

Moving the decision threshold trades sensitivity against specificity, since flagging more
messages catches more spam and misclassifies more clean mail. Improving both at once requires
a better model or more data. This block is [[STATISTICS]] under different names, and
[[Type I and Type II Errors]] carries the translation: a false positive is $\alpha$, a false
negative is $\beta$, and sensitivity is statistical power $1 - \beta$.

### Where the classification loss comes from

[[Information Theory]] defines the information in an event as $I(x) = -\log_2 P(x)$, so
[[Information]] is surprise and a certain event carries none. [[Entropy]] and
[[Shannon Entropy]] are the expected surprise, $H(P) = -\sum P(x)\log P(x)$, which is the
average number of bits an optimal code needs per symbol. A fair coin has entropy 1 bit and a
two-headed coin has entropy 0.

[[Cross-Entropy]] is $H(P,Q) = -\sum P(x)\log Q(x)$, the cost of coding data drawn from $P$
using a code built for $Q$, which is always at least $H(P)$. [[KL Divergence]] is the excess,
$D_{KL}(P\|Q) = H(P,Q) - H(P)$, and it is never negative.

Minimising cross-entropy over a fixed dataset minimises KL divergence, because $H(P)$ depends
only on the data and stays constant while the parameters move. Training a classifier on
cross-entropy loss is therefore driving the model's distribution toward the data's
distribution, which is the derivation behind the loss chosen in the section above.

### The linear algebra underneath

This material is borrowed from [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] and linked here.
[[Principal Component Analysis]] reduces dimension, and the route into it runs
[[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]], the [[Spectral Theorem]], the
[[Singular Value Decomposition]], then PCA. It is an eigendecomposition of a covariance
matrix, so it is [[Variance]] and eigenvectors applied to data. [[Vector Norm]] is where
regression losses come from, since squared $L_2$ is mean squared error. [[Least Squares]] is
the closed-form fit that gradient descent approaches iteratively, and [[NumPy]] is the array
library the code is written in.

## Related courses

- [[CALCULUS 1]] (MATH 1200) is the course this one runs on. [[Optimization]] owns the
  closed-form and iterative distinction, [[Chain Rule]] owns the mechanics of
  backpropagation, and [[Linear Approximation]] is what a gradient step performs.
- [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] (MATH 3200) supplies the [[Gradient]] and [[Partial Derivative]]
  that a derivative becomes with many inputs, and the [[Multivariable Chain Rule]] that
  [[Back Propagation]] sums over.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] (MATH 1203) supplies [[Matrix Multiplication]] for a forward pass,
  [[Dot Product]] for a neuron, and [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] for the start of the PCA
  chain.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303) owns
  [[Principal Component Analysis]], [[Vector Norm]], [[Least Squares]] and
  [[Image Processing]].
- [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234) is the statistical floor under this folder, holding
  [[Type I and Type II Errors]] for the evaluation table, [[Random Variable]] and
  [[Probability Distribution]] for expectation, the [[Bernoulli Distribution]] that
  [[Logistic Regression]] fits, the [[Sampling Distribution]] that explains why minibatches
  work, and [[Linear Regression]].
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] holds the neural network notes in `Books/`, covering the same
  material from the self-study side.
- [[ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE]] is the broader field this is one method inside. That course
  owns the agent, including search in [[A* Search]] and [[Heuristic]], decisions under
  uncertainty in [[Rational Agent]] and [[Expected Utility]], and learning from consequences
  in [[Reinforcement Learning]] and [[Q-Learning]]. It also owns [[Decision Tree]],
  [[Random Forest]] and [[Clustering]].
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] analyses gradient descent as an optimisation algorithm, and
  [[Time Complexity]] applies to training the same way it applies to sorting.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631) supplies the [[Tree]] a decision tree is and the
  [[Weighted Graph]] whose numbered edges a network mirrors.
- [[INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY AND SOCIETY]] (COMP 3309) treats the [[False Positive]] against
  [[False Negative]] choice as an ethical decision, since the two errors fall on different
  people.
- [[DIRECTED READING]] (COMP 4299) applies a language model to a live dataset, where
  [[LLM Grounding]] supplies the computed figures the model answers from.
